newsitem.title: EGYPT: Budding Cairo bourse looks at market makers to grow.
newsitem.headline: Budding Cairo bourse looks at market makers to grow.

text.p: Egypt's adolescent stock exchange needs the stabilising influence of market makers to mature, but stiff regulations and unsteady infrastructure are blocking the way, brokers and analysts say.

A recent presidential decree to shake up the bourse and the market's sharp rally and subsequent fall this year have attracted more followers to the market makers lobby, which includes some top bankers and brokers.

Market makers -- sellers or buyers of last resort -- concentrate their dealing activities on a choice stock. Their holdings of that stock help to regulate prices and smooth out any sharp fluctuations.

"Market makers enhance liquidity and investors will go where they can get in and out easily. These institutions give the confidence that when push comes to shove, they have someone to sell to and someone to buy from," said Mohammed Hossny, managing director of Triple A Securities.
Share prices on the Cairo bourse swung up 30 percent in the four weeks starting January 19 but the all-share index has since shed more than half those gains.

But while potential market makers and the state-run Capital Market Authority (CMA) agree on the benefits of such financial institutions, they cannot see eye-to-eye on how and when they will deal in the bourse.

CMA chief Abdel Hamid Ibrahim told Reuters he had invited brokers more than six months ago to set up market makers, but the brokers say lack of licences, an untidy bourse and an over-the-top capital requirement of 200 million pounds ($59 million) are effective deterrents.

"The bourse needs market makers, volume is increasing and they're all part of the market development," an international broker told Reuters. "But until the market is sorted out in many ways, it's difficult to think about them."

Teething problems continue to beset Egypt's fledgling market, which has attracted much international and local interest, particularly after investment-grade credit ratings by Standard and Poor's rating agency.
Most brokers complain about glitches in the automated dealing system, slow clearing procedures and other faulty technological infrastructure.
Others say the market does not have enough private firms outside the state's clutches to justify the expense of making a market in a certain stock.

"Market making is no joke," said Shereen ElKady, chief investment officer at analysts Prime Investments. "Millions are involved and we need to have a higher percentage of firms in which the state has privatised at least 75 percent."
Brokers argue that the 200 million pound capital stipulated by the CMA is too much for an emerging market like Egypt. They say only banks have that much money on hand.

"It's totally irrational to have so much capital. You don't need that much money to become a market maker, no one in Egypt has that much money anyway. The CMA are taking it too far," a prominent Egyptian broker said.
Mahmoud Abdel Aziz, chairman of the liberal state bank National Bank of Egypt, has called for diversification into market making but so far his pleas have fallen on deaf ears.
The root of the problem, the brokers say, is the state's attitude that everyone is a crook until proven otherwise.

"The CMA is afraid that people will play the market and that it will go berserk. Why assume the worst? They can easily avoid that by passing certain laws that will guarantee the safety of the market, but not having market makers is not the solution," the Egyptian broker added.
The lack of market makers in Egypt is not adversely affecting the bourse but their presence would help raise the market's profile, the brokers say.
"Not having market makers is not a bad thing, but they enhance liquidity, improve trading and having them sure helps," Hossny added.
